lessons.title: Reflect Points Across Axes
lessons.objective: I can reflect points across the x-axis and y-axis on the coordinate plane.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words reflection, x-axis, y-axis, and symmetry.

concept.heading: How do you reflect a point across an axis?
concept.intro: A reflection is a flip of a point over a line, like a mirror image. The axis you flip over decides which coordinate changes its sign.
concept.keyIdea: Reflections Across Axes. Formula: Reflect over x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y) | Reflect over y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y). 1. Reflection across x-axis (horizontal line): y-coordinate changes sign, x stays same. 2. Reflection across y-axis (vertical line): x-coordinate changes sign, y stays same. 3. Both coordinates change sign when reflecting across both axes: (−x, −y)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I will reflect (3, 2) over the y-axis.
The y-axis is the vertical line, so the point flips left or right. That changes the x-coordinate.
The x changes sign: 3 becomes -3. The y stays the same: 2 stays 2.
So the reflection of (3, 2) over the y-axis is (-3, 2).
linesEs: Voy a reflejar (3, 2) sobre el eje y.
El eje y es la línea vertical, así que el punto se voltea a la izquierda o a la derecha. Eso cambia la coordenada x.
La x cambia de signo: 3 se vuelve -3. La y queda igual: 2 sigue siendo 2.
Entonces la reflexión de (3, 2) sobre el eje y es (-3, 2).

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Now let's reflect (4, -5) over the x-axis. Which coordinate changes over the x-axis? The y-coordinate.
What does -5 become when it changes sign? It becomes 5.
The x stays 4, so the reflection is what point? It is (4, 5).
linesEs: Ahora reflejemos (4, -5) sobre el eje x. ¿Qué coordenada cambia con el eje x? La coordenada y.
¿En qué se convierte -5 cuando cambia de signo? Se vuelve 5.
La x sigue siendo 4, entonces ¿cuál es el punto reflejado? Es (4, 5).

vocabulary.definition: Flip a point across an axis so it stays the same perpendicular distance from that axis.
A flipped, mirror image across a line.
vocabulary.example: (3, 2) reflected over the y-axis becomes (-3, 2) — x changes sign, y stays

vocabulary.definition: The line that goes across the grid. Flipping over it changes the y sign.
vocabulary.example: (4, 3) → (4, -3): the y flips from +3 to -3, like folding the paper along the horizontal line

vocabulary.definition: The line that goes up the grid. Flipping over it changes the x sign.
vocabulary.example: (4, 3) → (-4, 3): the x flips from +4 to -4, like folding the paper along the vertical line

vocabulary.definition: When a shape looks the same on both sides of a line.
vocabulary.example: A butterfly's wings are symmetric — fold it down the middle and both sides match

vocabulary.definition: Whole numbers and their opposites, like -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.
Two lines that meet to make a square corner (90 degrees).
vocabulary.example: The dashed height meets the base at a square corner — the small 90° box is what makes it perpendicular, not slanted.

title: Mirror Mission
mission: Send a point through coordinate mirrors. Predict which coordinate changes and prove that reflected points stay equally far from the mirror.
investigate: Reflect (−3, 4) across the y-axis, then across the x-axis.
Find a point that does not move when reflected across the x-axis.
Explain why negating both coordinates is not a single reflection across one axis.
create: Create a four-point emblem and reflect it across each axis. Give the image coordinates and explain how distance from the mirror proves your construction.

support.prompt: What is the reflection of (4, -3) over the x-axis?
support.explanation: Reflecting over the x-axis changes the sign of the y-coordinate. The x stays the same (4), and the y changes from -3 to 3. The answer is (4, 3).
feedback: That is what you get if you changed the sign of both coordinates. Instead: Reflecting over the x-axis changes the sign of the y-coordinate.
Both coordinates changed sign here, which is what two reflections would do. A single reflection over the x-axis leaves one coordinate untouched — decide which one.
The two numbers traded places. Reflecting never swaps x with y; it only changes a sign.
hints: Reflecting over the x-axis flips the point UP/DOWN — the left/right position doesn't move.
Keep the x-coordinate the same and switch the sign of the y-coordinate. Don't swap the numbers' order.
The point sits 3 units below the x-axis. Its mirror sits the same 3 units above, with the x still 4.

support.prompt: What is the reflection of (-2, 6) over the y-axis?
support.explanation: Reflecting over the y-axis changes the sign of the x-coordinate. x goes from -2 to 2, and y stays 6. The answer is (2, 6).
feedback: That is what you get if you changed the sign of both coordinates. Instead: Reflecting over the y-axis changes the sign of the x-coordinate.
Both signs flipped in this point. A reflection over the y-axis changes only one coordinate — think about which one the vertical axis affects.
The coordinates were swapped instead of reflected. Keep x in the first position and y in the second, then change only a sign.
hints: Reflecting over the y-axis flips LEFT/RIGHT — the height stays the same.
Switch the sign of the x-coordinate and keep the y-coordinate 6 unchanged.
The point is 2 units left of the y-axis. Its mirror lands 2 units to the RIGHT, at the same height.

support.prompt: Which point is on the y-axis?
support.explanation: Points on the y-axis have x-coordinate = 0. (0, 5) is on the y-axis.
feedback: That point sits off to one side of the vertical axis. A point resting on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of exactly 0.
Not quite. Points on the y-axis have x-coordinate = ___.
You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
hints: Points on the y-axis have gone 0 units left or right — check the FIRST coordinate.
Scan each pair's x-coordinate (the first number). Only x = 0 keeps a point on the y-axis.
Read the first number in each pair. A point sits on the y-axis only when that number is 0.

steps: Problem: Reflect the point (6, 4) over the y-axis.
Attempt: The y-axis is vertical, so I will change the y-coordinate: 4 becomes -4. The answer is (6, -4).
Check: The point only moved up and down, but a fold over the vertical y-axis should move it left and right.
support.explanation: Reflecting over the y-axis changes the x-coordinate, not the y-coordinate. The rule is (x, y) -> (-x, y). For (6, 4), flip x: 6 becomes -6, and keep y as 4. The correct reflection is (-6, 4), not (6, -4).
hints: The y-axis is the vertical line. Folding over it moves a point left or right, so the x-coordinate is what changes.
Over the y-axis: (x, y) -> (-x, y). So (6, 4) becomes (-6, 4), not (6, -4).

core.prompt: Point A is at (-3, 5). It is reflected over the x-axis to A', then A' is reflected over the y-axis to A''. What are the coordinates of A''?
core.explanation: Over x-axis: (-3, 5) → (-3, -5). Then over y-axis: (-3, -5) → (3, -5). Both coordinates changed sign.
feedback: The first coordinate at origin is not 1.
One coordinate is correct, but check the other.
Both coordinates at origin are the same value — 0.
hints: Two flips happen in a row — do them one at a time, not both at once.
The first flip (x-axis) changes only the y sign. Then flip THAT result over the y-axis, changing only the x sign.
Step 1: (-3, 5) over the x-axis — keep the -3 and flip the 5. Carry that new point into the second reflection.

steps: Problem: Reflect the point (-3, -8) over the x-axis.
Attempt: Both coordinates are negative, so I will flip the x-coordinate: -3 becomes 3. The answer is (3, -8).
Check: Folding over the horizontal x-axis should send the point up across the axis, but this answer kept it below the axis.
core.explanation: Reflecting over the x-axis changes the y-coordinate, not the x-coordinate. The rule is (x, y) -> (x, -y). For (-3, -8), keep x as -3 and flip y: -8 becomes 8. The correct reflection is (-3, 8), not (3, -8). The negative signs do not change which coordinate flips — the axis does.
hints: The x-axis is the horizontal line. Folding over it moves a point up or down, so the y-coordinate is what changes sign.
Over the x-axis: (x, y) -> (x, -y). So (-3, -8) becomes (-3, 8), not (3, -8).

steps: Student thinking: The y-axis is vertical, so I change the y-coordinate
stretch.explanation: Reflecting over the y-axis changes the x-coordinate, not the y-coordinate. The correct reflection of (-3, 5) over the y-axis is (3, 5). The student confused which coordinate changes for each axis.
hints: The y-AXIS is the vertical line. Points flip ACROSS it, meaning they move left/right. Which coordinate controls left/right?
Over the y-axis: change x. Over the x-axis: change y. The name of the axis tells you which coordinate STAYS the same.

stretch.prompt: A triangle has vertices at A(1, 2), B(4, 2), and C(4, 6). If you reflect the entire triangle over the y-axis, what are the new vertices? What do you notice about the size and shape of the reflected triangle compared to the original?
stretch.frame: The reflected vertices are A'(___), B'(___), C'(___). I found each by ___. The reflected triangle is ___ compared to the original because reflections ___.
stretch.explanation: Reflect each vertex over the y-axis by flipping only the x-coordinate: A(1, 2) → A'(-1, 2), B(4, 2) → B'(-4, 2), and C(4, 6) → C'(-4, 6). The reflected triangle is congruent to the original — same side lengths and same angles — because a reflection is a mirror flip that turns the figure around without stretching or shrinking it.
hints: Reflect each vertex separately over the y-axis: only the x-coordinates change sign.
Apply the rule to A(1, 2), B(4, 2), and C(4, 6) one at a time. Then compare the side lengths of both triangles.
Start with A(1, 2): flip the 1 to its opposite and keep the 2. Do B and C the same way, then compare shapes.
